newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FCC chief seeks cut in global phone rates.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FCC chief seeks cut in global phone rates.

text.p: The nation's top communications regulator said on Wednesday his agency would step up efforts to force state-run phone monopolies overseas to reduce what they charge U.S. companies to complete overseas phone calls.

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt also charged that Asian nations continue to drag their feet over offers to open their telecommunications markets during World Trade Organisation negotiations.

Speaking to the Institute for International Economics, Hundt said the FCC would unveil plans in about a month designed to drive down the cost of international accounting rates levied on U.S. carriers to complete overseas calls.
"We are suggesting some pretty radical overhauls of the world's accounting system," Hundt said.
He declined to give details about the plan, saying only the FCC was prepared to offer "benchmark" rates for what it considers to be appropriate accounting rate levels.
He vowed the agency would be aggressive in pursuing a cut in overseas rates to levels that better reflect costs.
The FCC has complained the differences in rates between the United States and other nations resulted in an outflow of payments from this country to overseas of more than $4 billion in 1994.
Referring to the WTO talks, Hundt said several Asian nations have "got to make better offers and they have to make more offers" for opening their communications markets to competition.
He singled out India, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Hong Kong, Singapore, the Philippines and South Korea as not going far enough.
